verses.translation: And the fifth{H2549} messenger{H4397} sounded{H8628}, and I saw{H7200} one{H259} star{H3556} falling{H5307} upon the earth{H776} from the heavens{H8064}; and to him was given{H5414} the key{H4668} of the Deep{H8415}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תּוֹקֵעַ (toqea, H8628) — the specific Torah word for ritual blowing of the shofar (Num 10:3-7, Josh 6:4,9,13, Judg 3:27, 7:18). Greek ἐσάλπισεν simply means 'trumpeted.' The Hebrew naturally reaches for the Torah's ritual-blowing term; a back-translator would use a generic verb.

Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom, H8415 — 'the Deep') — the primordial deep of Genesis 1:2 (וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי תְהוֹם). Greek has τῆς ἀβύσσου ('the abyss'). The Hebrew word evokes the pre-creation chaos waters. A back-translator from ἄβυσσος would likely transliterate or use a different term, not reach for the Genesis cosmological word. The brackets [   ] in the source suggest a lacuna where Greek has 'the pit of the abyss' (τοῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσου) — the Hebrew is more concise, simply 'of the Deep.'
greek_deviations: Greek: 'the key of the pit of the abyss' (κλεὶς τοῦ φρέατος τῆς ἀβύσσου). Hebrew: 'the key of the Deep' (המפתח מתהום). Greek adds 'pit' (φρέαρ); the Hebrew has only 'the Deep.'
translation_notes: 'The Deep' for tehom preserves the Genesis 1:2 cosmological connection — the same primordial waters that existed before creation.
Brackets in the source text indicate missing text likely corresponding to Greek 'pit of.'
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — וְחֹשֶׁךְ עַל פְּנֵי תְהוֹם ('and darkness was upon the face of the Deep'). The tehom is the primordial chaos that precedes ordered creation. The Hebrew author sees the abyss not as a Greek mythological underworld but as the Genesis pre-creation void.

verses.translation: And he opened{H6605} the Deep{H8415}, and smoke{H6227} went out{H3318} from the Deep{H8415} like smoke{H6227} from a great{H1419} furnace{H8574}; and the sun{H8121} and the air were darkened{H2821} from the smoke{H6227} of the Deep{H8415}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom) THREE times in a single verse — a concentrated repetition emphasizing the Genesis cosmological dimension. Greek varies between φρέαρ ('pit') and ἄβυσσος ('abyss'). The Hebrew hammers the single primordial term.

Uses תַּנּוּר (tannur, H8574 — 'furnace/oven') — the word from Abraham's covenant vision in Genesis 15:17 (תַּנּוּר עָשָׁן — 'a smoking furnace') and the prophetic judgment imagery of Malachi 4:1. Greek uses κάμινος (generic furnace). A back-translator would not specifically choose the Abraham-covenant furnace word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew opens 'the Deep' directly (פתח התהום); Greek opens 'the pit of the abyss' (τὸ φρέαρ τῆς ἀβύσσου) — again adding 'pit' as a distinct structure.
Hebrew repeats 'the Deep' (תהום) three times for rhetorical emphasis. Greek varies its terminology.
translation_notes: 'Furnace' for tannur — the covenant/judgment furnace of Genesis 15:17 and Malachi 4:1.
אֲוִיר (avir — 'air') is a post-biblical Hebrew term without a standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Genesis 15:17 — 'And behold, a smoking furnace (תנור עשן) and a flaming torch that passed between those pieces.' The covenant-furnace imagery links this judgment to the Abrahamic covenant.

verses.translation: And from the smoke{H6227} came{H935} locusts{H697} upon the earth{H776}, and to them was given{H5414} authority to destroy{H7843}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַרְבָּהִים (arbahim) — an unusual plural of אַרְבֶּה (arbeh, H697 — 'locust'). The locust is the eighth plague of Egypt (Ex 10:4-19) and Joel's apocalyptic army (Joel 1:4, 2:25). Greek ἀκρίδες is generic 'locusts.' The Hebrew connects these creatures directly to the Exodus plague tradition.

Uses לְהַשְׁחִית (lehashchit — 'to destroy', Hiphil of שׁחת H7843) — the specific verb God uses for the Flood: 'I am about to destroy them' (Gen 6:13 — מַשְׁחִיתָם), and for the destruction of Sodom (Gen 13:10, 19:13). Greek has ἐξουσίαν ὡς ἔχουσιν ἐξουσίαν οἱ σκορπίοι ('authority as the scorpions have authority') — an entirely different statement. The Hebrew says 'authority to destroy'; the Greek compares authority to scorpions. A back-translator from Greek would not use the Flood/Sodom verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'authority to destroy' (רשות להשחית). Greek: 'authority as the scorpions of the earth have authority' (ἐξουσίαν ὡς ἔχουσιν ἐξουσίαν οἱ σκορπίοι τῆς γῆς). Entirely different construction — one states purpose, the other makes a comparison.
Brackets in the Hebrew source around both 'locusts' and near 'authority' suggest editorial restorations or lacunae.
translation_notes: רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority/permission') is a post-biblical Hebrew term common in Mishnaic Hebrew. No standard Strong's number.
textual_notes: Joel 1:4 — 'What the cutting locust left, the swarming locust (ארבה) ate.' Joel 2:25 — 'I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust (ארבה) has eaten.' The Hebrew author draws from the Joel tradition of locusts as instruments of divine judgment.

verses.translation: And it was said{H559} to them that they should not harm the greenery{H3419} or the herb{H6212} of the field{H7704}, or any tree{H6086}; only the sons{H1121} of Adam{H120} who do not have the seals upon their foreheads{H4696} from YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יֶרֶק (yereq, H3419 — 'greenery') and עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה ('herb of the field', H6212+H7704) — Genesis creation vocabulary. Gen 1:30: 'every green herb' (כָּל יֶרֶק עֵשֶׂב). Gen 2:5: 'every herb of the field' (כָּל עֵשֶׂב הַשָּׂדֶה). The Hebrew author draws on the creation narrative's specific botanical terminology. Greek uses χόρτον ('grass') and χλωρόν ('green thing') — more generic terms. A back-translator from Greek would use דֶּשֶׁא (deshe — 'grass'), not the Genesis pair yereq/esev.

Uses חֲתִימֹת מִיַּהְוֶה ('seals from YHWH') — from the root חתם (chatam, H2856 — 'to seal'), used for sealing documents and covenants (1 Kings 21:8, Neh 9:38, Dan 12:4). Greek says 'the seal of God' (σφραγῖδα τοῦ θεοῦ) — singular where Hebrew has plural, and generic θεός where Hebrew has the specific covenant name YHWH. A back-translator from Greek would never independently choose the Tetragrammaton.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'greenery and herb of the field' (ירק ועשב השדה). Greek: 'the grass of the earth nor any green thing' (χόρτον τῆς γῆς οὐδὲ πᾶν χλωρόν). Different vegetation terms and 'field' vs. 'earth.'
Hebrew: 'seals from YHWH' (חתימות מיהוה — plural, with YHWH). Greek: 'the seal of God' (σφραγῖδα τοῦ θεοῦ — singular, with θεός). Different number and divine name.
translation_notes: תַּזִּיקוּ (tazziku — 'you shall harm') is from the root נזק, common in Mishnaic Hebrew but not standard in the OT. No Strong's number.
חֲתִימֹת (chatimot — 'seals') is a post-biblical plural noun form from חתם. No standard Strong's for this nominal form.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 9:4 — 'Go through the midst of the city... and set a mark (תָו) upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations.' The Hebrew concept of a divine mark/seal on foreheads protecting the righteous from judgment is rooted in Ezekiel.

verses.translation: And to them was given{H5414} not to kill{H4191} them, only to afflict them five{H2568} months{H2320}; and their affliction was as the affliction of scorpions{H6137} when one bites{H5391}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נוֹשֵׁךְ (noshech — 'bites', H5391) for the scorpion's sting. This is the same root used for the serpent's bite in Genesis 49:17 (נֹשֵׁךְ עִקְּבֵי סוּס — 'biting the horse's heels') and the fiery serpents of Numbers 21:6-9. The word also means 'to charge interest' (Deut 23:20) — literally 'biting' someone financially. Greek παίσῃ simply means 'strikes.' The Hebrew connects the scorpion-plague to the serpent imagery of Torah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'when one bites' (באם שנושך — serpent-bite language). Greek: 'when it strikes a man' (ὅταν παίσῃ ἄνθρωπον — generic striking).
translation_notes: צַעֵר/צַעַר (tsa'er/tsa'ar — 'afflict/affliction') is post-biblical Hebrew. No standard Strong's number. Greek uses βασανίζω ('torment/torture').

verses.translation: And in those{H1992} days{H3117} they shall seek death{H4194} and shall not find{H4672} it.

greek_deviations: Hebrew is much shorter — only 'they shall seek death and not find it.' Greek adds an entire second clause: 'and shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them' (καὶ ἐπιθυμήσουσιν ἀποθανεῖν, καὶ φεύξεται ὁ θάνατος ἀπ' αὐτῶν). The personification of death fleeing is absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: תַּחְכִּימוּ — morphologically unusual. Possibly an intensive form from the root חכה (chakhah, H2442 — 'to wait/long for'), or a textual variant. The contextual meaning 'to seek/long for' is clear and matches Greek ζητήσουσιν ('they shall seek').

verses.translation: And the locusts{H697} were like horses{H5483} prepared{H3559} for battle{H4421}, and upon their heads{H7218} the likeness{H1823} of crowns{H3804} of gold{H2091}, and their appearances{H4758} like the appearances of a man{H120}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כִּדְמוּת (kidmut — 'in the likeness of', H1823) — the creation term from Genesis 1:26 (נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ — 'Let us make man in our image, in our likeness'). The Hebrew naturally reaches for this theologically loaded word. Greek uses ὡς στέφανοι ὅμοιοι ('like crowns similar to'). A back-translator from Greek would not choose the Genesis creation term.

DIRECT ECHO of Joel 2:4: כְּמַרְאֵה סוּסִים מַרְאֵהוּ ('like the appearance of horses is their appearance'). The Hebrew Revelation's locust-horse comparison and the precise phrasing מראיהם כמראות reproduce Joel's apocalyptic locust army imagery. A back-translator from Greek would have no reason to reproduce the Joel phrasing.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the locusts were like horses' (ארבהים כמו הסוסים). Greek: 'the likenesses of the locusts were like horses' (τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν ἀκρίδων ὅμοια ἵπποις). Greek adds an extra layer of abstraction with 'likenesses.'
translation_notes: כִּתְרֵי (kitrei — 'crowns of') is the construct plural of כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804), appearing in the OT only in Esther (1:11, 2:17, 6:8). A Persian-period word for royal crown.
textual_notes: Joel 2:4-5 — 'Their appearance is like the appearance of horses; like horsemen, so they run. Like the noise of chariots on the tops of mountains they leap.' The Joel parallel extends beyond appearance to the full military imagery.

verses.translation: And their hair{H8181} was like the hair{H8181} of women{H802}, and its teeth{H8127} like the teeth{H8127} of a lion{H738}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT ECHO of Joel 1:6: שִׁנָּיו שִׁנֵּי אַרְיֵה ('its teeth are the teeth of a lion'). The Hebrew switches from plural 'their hair' (שַׂעֲרוֹתֵיהֶם) to singular 'its teeth' (שִׁנָּיו) — exactly as Joel does, treating the locust swarm collectively as a single entity. Greek maintains plural throughout (οἱ ὀδόντες αὐτῶν — 'their teeth'). A back-translator from Greek, seeing plural 'their teeth,' would never switch to Joel's singular.
greek_deviations: Hebrew switches from plural 'their hair' to singular 'its teeth' (echoing Joel 1:6). Greek maintains plural consistently.
translation_notes: 'Its teeth' (singular suffix) preserved in translation to show the Joel 1:6 verbatim echo.
textual_notes: Joel 1:6 — 'For a nation has come up against my land, powerful and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion (שִׁנָּיו שִׁנֵּי אַרְיֵה), and it has the fangs of a lioness.' The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Joel's exact phrase.

verses.translation: And their tails{H2180} were like the tails{H2180} of a locust{H697}, and to them was given{H5414} authority to afflict the sons{H1121} of Adam{H120} five{H2568} months{H2320}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'tails like a locust' (כְּזַנְבֵי אַרְבֶּה). Greek (v10): 'tails like scorpions' (οὐρὰς ὁμοίας σκορπίοις). The Hebrew compares the tails to LOCUST tails, maintaining the arbeh identity throughout the passage. The Greek switches to SCORPION tails. A back-translator from Greek would write כְּזַנְבוֹת עַקְרַבִּים ('like scorpion tails'), not 'locust tails.' The Hebrew author consistently identifies these creatures as locusts — the Exodus/Joel plague creature.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tails like a locust' (כזנבי ארבה). Greek (v10): 'tails like scorpions, and stings were in their tails' (οὐρὰς ὁμοίας σκορπίοις καὶ κέντρα). Different creature reference, and Greek adds 'stings' which is absent from Hebrew.

The entire content of Greek v9 — breastplates of iron, the sound of wings like many chariots rushing to battle (θώρακας ὡς θώρακας σιδηροῦς, καὶ ἡ φωνὴ τῶν πτερύγων αὐτῶν ὡς φωνὴ ἁρμάτων) — is ABSENT from the Hebrew text.
translation_notes: The Hebrew maintains locust imagery (ארבה) consistently, while the Greek alternates between locusts and scorpions. This suggests independent traditions rather than translation.

verses.translation: And their king{H4428} was one{H259} messenger{H4397} from the Deep{H8415}, and his name{H8034} in the Hebrew{H5680} tongue{H3956} is Avadon{H11}, and in the tongue{H3956} of Yavan{H3120} Apollyon.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The direction of explanation flows Hebrew→Greek. The author FIRST gives the Hebrew name אֲבַדּוֹן (Avadon, H11) — a NATIVE Hebrew word for the realm of destruction/death appearing six times in the OT (Job 26:6, 28:22, 31:12; Ps 88:12; Prov 15:11, 27:20) — and THEN provides the Greek equivalent for non-Hebrew readers. If this were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would give the Greek name first and the Hebrew as an explanation. The direction of explanation is the direction of composition.

Uses יָוָן (Yavan, H3120) for 'Greece' — the biblical Hebrew geographic name from the Table of Nations (Gen 10:2, son of Yefet) and Daniel's prophecy (Dan 8:21, 10:20, 11:2). A back-translator from Greek would say בְּיוּנִית ('in Greek') or Ἑλληνικῇ transliterated, not use the Torah's genealogical name for the Greek people.
Uses מִתְּהוֹם ('from the Deep') again — consistently tehom rather than any other underworld term. Greek has τῆς ἀβύσσου ('of the abyss').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the Hebrew tongue... in the tongue of Yavan' (בלשון עברי... בלשון יון). Greek: 'in Hebrew... in Greek' (Ἑβραϊστί... ἐν τῇ Ἑλληνικῇ). The Hebrew uses native geographic terminology; the Greek uses Greek adverbs.
translation_notes: 'Avadon' transliterated rather than translated to preserve the proper name. The Hebrew root אבד (avad) means 'to perish/be destroyed.'
'Yavan' for Greece follows biblical Hebrew convention (Gen 10:2, Dan 8:21).
textual_notes: Job 26:6 — 'Sheol is naked before him, and Avadon (אֲבַדּוֹן) has no covering.' Job 28:22 — 'Avadon and Death say, We have heard a rumor of it with our ears.' In the OT, Avadon is personified as a realm parallel to Sheol and Death.

verses.translation: One{H259} woe has gone{H1980}; see{H7200}, two{H8147} more woes are coming{H935}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כְּאֵב (ke'ev — 'pain/grief', related to H3511) for 'woe.' This Hebrew word carries a physical-pain connotation — the anguish of bodily suffering (Job 2:13, Jer 15:18). Greek οὐαί is an abstract interjection ('alas!'). The Hebrew turns the woe into a concrete experience of pain. A back-translator from Greek would use הוֹי (hoy — 'woe!', the prophetic interjection) or אוֹי (oy), not the physical-pain word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'one woe has gone' (אחד כעב הלך). Greek: 'the first woe has passed; behold, the two woes come after these things' (Ἡ οὐαὶ ἡ μία ἀπῆλθεν· ἰδού, ἔρχονται ἔτι δύο οὐαὶ μετὰ ταῦτα). Greek adds 'after these things.'
translation_notes: כְּעֵב/כְּאֵב — variant spelling of the noun from root כאב (ka'av, H3510 — 'to be in pain'). The interchange of א and ע is common in late Hebrew.

verses.translation: And the sixth{H8345} messenger{H4397} sounded{H8628}, and I heard{H8085} one{H259} voice{H6963} from the four{H702} corners{H6438} of the Temple{H1964} before{H6440} YHWH{H3068}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses פִּינּוֹת הַהֵיכָל ('corners of the Temple', H6438+H1964). Greek has τῶν τεσσάρων κεράτων τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου τοῦ χρυσοῦ ('the four horns of the golden altar'). These are entirely different structures — the Hebrew envisions the architectural corners of the Temple building; the Greek envisions the horn-projections of the golden incense altar. A back-translator from Greek would write קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ הַזָּהָב ('horns of the golden altar'), not 'corners of the Temple.'

Uses הֵיכָל (heikhal, H1964) — the OT's word for the main Temple hall (1 Kings 6:3,5,17; Ps 5:8, 11:4, 18:7). This is the architectural term for the building itself, not furniture within it. The Greek specifies altar furniture; the Hebrew specifies the sacred building.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ). The Hebrew uses the specific covenant name.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'four corners of the Temple' (ארבע פינות ההיכל). Greek: 'four horns of the golden altar' (τεσσάρων κεράτων τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου τοῦ χρυσοῦ). Entirely different sacred structure.
Hebrew: 'before YHWH' (לפני יהוה). Greek: 'before God' (ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ). Different divine designation.
translation_notes: פִּנָּה (pinnah, H6438 — 'corner') is used for the corners of buildings, the cornerstone (Ps 118:22, Isa 28:16), and the 'four corners' of the earth (Isa 11:12). The voice emanates from the very structure of the Temple.

verses.translation: And it said{H559} to the sixth{H8345} messenger{H4397} who sounded{H8628}: Go{H1980} and search{H2664} for the four{H702} messengers{H4397} who are bound{H631} beside{H681} the great{H1419} sea{H3220} which is called{H7121} Euphrates{H6578}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל ('the great sea', H3220+H1419) for what Greek calls ποταμῷ τῷ μεγάλῳ Εὐφράτῃ ('the great RIVER Euphrates'). The Hebrew calls the Euphrates a יָם (yam — 'sea'), not a נָהָר (nahar — 'river'). In OT usage, 'the great sea' (הַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל) is the standard designation for the Mediterranean (Num 34:6-7, Josh 1:4, 9:1, 15:12). A back-translator from Greek 'river' (ποταμός) would write nahar, not yam. The Hebrew author's use of 'sea' for the Euphrates reflects ancient Near Eastern cosmological language where great waters carry chaos associations.

Uses לֵךְ וְחַפֵּשׁ ('go and search for', H1980+H2664). Greek says Λῦσον ('loose/release'). The Hebrew commands a SEARCH mission; the Greek commands a RELEASE. A back-translator from Greek would write הַתֵּר ('loose') or שַׁחְרֵר ('release'), not 'go and search.' The Hebrew implies the bound angels must first be located before they can be released.

Uses אֲסוּרִים (asurim — 'bound/imprisoned', from אסר H631) — the standard OT word for prisoners (Gen 39:20, 40:3,5; Isa 42:7, 49:9, 61:1). The same root appears in Isaiah's liberation prophecy: 'to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out prisoners (אסורים) from the dungeon.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the great sea called Euphrates' (הים הגדול הנקרא פרת). Greek: 'the great river Euphrates' (ποταμῷ τῷ μεγάλῳ Εὐφράτῃ). Sea vs. river — fundamentally different geographic conception.
Hebrew: 'go and search for' (לך וחפש). Greek: 'loose' (Λῦσον). Search mission vs. release command.
translation_notes: The qualifying phrase הַנִּקְרָא פְּרָת ('which is called Euphrates') suggests the author is clarifying which 'great sea' is meant — as if the designation might not be immediately obvious. This is consistent with the unusual identification of the Euphrates as a 'sea.'
textual_notes: Genesis 15:18 — 'To your seed I have given this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (עַד הַנָּהָר הַגָּדֹל נְהַר פְּרָת).' In the Torah, the Euphrates is called a נָהָר (nahar — 'river'), never a יָם (yam — 'sea'). The Hebrew Revelation's deliberate use of 'sea' is a theological choice connecting the Euphrates to cosmic-chaos waters.

verses.translation: And the four{H702} messengers{H4397} were prepared{H3559} to kill{H4191} a third{H7992} of the sons{H1121} of Adam{H120}, in one{H259} hour{H8160} and day{H3117} and month{H2320} and year{H8141}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בְּנֵי אָדָם ('sons of Adam', H1121+H120) consistently throughout the chapter rather than a generic word for 'people.' This perpetually links humanity back to Genesis — we are always Adam's children. Greek uses τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('mankind') without the genealogical connection.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in one hour and day and month and year' (using the preposition ב on each time word, with אחד at the end). Greek: 'for THE hour and day and month and year' (εἰς τὴν ὥραν καὶ ἡμέραν καὶ μῆνα καὶ ἐνιαυτόν — using the article). The Hebrew implies a measured duration; the Greek implies a specific appointed time.
translation_notes: שָׁעָה (sha'ah — 'hour/moment', H8160) in this sense is Aramaic-influenced, as in Daniel 3:6, 4:16.

verses.translation: And their chariotry{H7393} numbered{H4557} two myriads{H7233} of thousands{H505}, and I heard{H8085} their number{H4557}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רִכְבֵיהֶם (richveihem — 'their chariotry', from rechev H7393) — the standard OT word for war chariots (Ex 14:7, Josh 11:4, Judg 4:3, 1 Kings 10:26, 2 Kings 6:17 — Elisha's chariots of fire). Greek uses στρατευμάτων τοῦ ἱππικοῦ ('armies of cavalry/horsemen'). A back-translator from Greek would use פָּרָשִׁים (parashim — 'horsemen/cavalry'), not the chariot-specific rechev. The Hebrew envisions chariot warfare in the OT tradition; the Greek envisions mounted cavalry.

The number is רִבֹּתַיִם אַלְפֵי ('two myriads of thousands'). Greek has δύο μυριάδες μυριάδων ('two myriads of myriads' = 200 million). The Hebrew number (two ten-thousands of thousands) is vastly different from the Greek 200 million. These cannot be translation variants — they represent independent numerical traditions.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'chariotry' (רכב — war chariots). Greek: 'cavalry armies' (στρατευμάτων τοῦ ἱππικοῦ — mounted troops). Different military units.
Hebrew: 'two myriads of thousands' (רבתים אלפי). Greek: 'two myriads of myriads' (δύο μυριάδες μυριάδων). Different numbers entirely.
translation_notes: רִבֹּתַיִם (ribbotayim) is the dual form of רְבָבָה (revavah, H7233 — 'myriad/ten thousand'). The dual = 20,000. With אַלְפֵי ('thousands'), the total could be 'twenty thousands' = 20,000 or 'twenty-thousand-fold thousands.'
textual_notes: 2 Kings 6:17 — 'And YHWH opened the eyes of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots (רכב) of fire.' The Hebrew author's use of rechev connects this supernatural army to Elisha's vision of YHWH's heavenly chariot force.

verses.translation: And after{H310} this I saw{H7200} in the form of the horses{H5483} and those sitting{H3427} upon them, who had garments{H4403} of pitch{H2203} and sulfur{H1614} and fire{H784}; and the heads{H7218} of the horses{H5483} were like the heads{H7218} of a lion{H738}, and from their mouths{H6310} went{H1980} fire{H784} and smoke{H6227} and sulfur{H1614}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זֶפֶת (zefet, H2203 — 'pitch/tar') where Greek has ὑακινθίνους ('jacinth/hyacinth-blue'). Pitch is black tar — the substance used to coat Moses' basket (Ex 2:3 — וַתַּחְמְרָה בַחֵמָר וּבַזָּפֶת) and the judgment substance of Edom (Isa 34:9 — 'her streams shall be turned into pitch'). These are entirely different substances. The Hebrew author clothes the riders in Sodom/Edom judgment materials. A back-translator from Greek 'jacinth' would never write 'pitch.'

Uses מַלְבּוּשִׁים (malbushim — 'garments/clothing', H4403) where Greek has θώρακας ('breastplates/armor'). A back-translator from Greek would use שִׁרְיוֹן (shiryon — 'armor/breastplate'), not the general word for clothing. The Hebrew envisions riders CLOTHED in pitch, sulfur, and fire — dressed in the instruments of divine judgment, like the consuming fire of Sodom (Gen 19:24).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'garments of pitch and sulfur and fire' (מלבושים של זפת וגפרית ואש). Greek: 'breastplates of fire and jacinth and sulfur' (θώρακας πυρίνους καὶ ὑακινθίνους καὶ θειώδεις). Garments vs. breastplates, and pitch vs. jacinth.
Hebrew brackets [  ] between 'lion heads' and 'from their mouths' suggest missing text.
translation_notes: The combination of pitch (זפת), sulfur (גפרית), and fire (אש) echoes the destruction of Sodom — Gen 19:24: 'Then YHWH rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah sulfur (גפרית) and fire (אש).' Isaiah 34:9 adds pitch (זפת) to the judgment materials. The Hebrew author clothes the riders in the full arsenal of divine judgment.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:9 — 'And her streams shall be turned into pitch (זפת), and her dust into sulfur (גפרית), and her land shall become burning pitch.' The Hebrew triad of pitch-sulfur-fire is an Isaiah/Genesis judgment motif.

verses.translation: And from these three{H7969} was killed{H2026} a third{H7992} of the sons{H1121} of Adam{H120}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from these three was killed' (concise, six words). Greek adds an expanded explanation: 'by the fire and the smoke and the sulfur going out of their mouths' (ἐκ τοῦ πυρὸς καὶ τοῦ καπνοῦ καὶ τοῦ θείου τοῦ ἐκπορευομένου ἐκ τῶν στομάτων αὐτῶν). The Hebrew is characteristically terse; the Greek is characteristically explanatory.
Hebrew: 'from these three' (מאילו השלושה — the three substances). Greek: 'by these three plagues' (ὑπὸ τῶν τριῶν πληγῶν τούτων). Greek adds the word 'plagues.'
translation_notes: נֶהֱרַג (neherag — 'was killed', Niphal of הרג H2026) — the strong verb for killing/slaying used from Cain onward (Gen 4:8, 34:25, Ex 2:14).

verses.translation: For their power{H3581} was in their mouths{H6310}, and their tails{H2180} were like serpents{H5175} and had heads{H7218}; and with these they kill{H2026} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֹּחַ (koach — 'power/strength', H3581) where Greek has ἐξουσία ('authority'). These are fundamentally different concepts: koach is raw power/might (Gen 4:12 — the ground's power; Ex 9:16 — God's power; Deut 8:17 — 'my power made me this wealth'). Exousia is delegated authority/permission. A back-translator from Greek exousia would use רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority') or שִׁלְטוֹן (shilton — 'dominion'), not the raw-might word koach.

Uses נְחָשִׁים (nechashim — 'serpents', H5175) — THE word for the serpent of Eden (Gen 3:1), the fiery serpents in the wilderness (Num 21:6-9), and prophetic serpent imagery (Isa 27:1). The Eden/serpent theology permeates this imagery. Greek uses ὄφεσιν ('snakes'). Both mean serpent, but the Hebrew form carries the full weight of Torah serpent theology — from Eden's nachash to the bronze nachash of healing.

Hebrew: 'with these they KILL them' (הורגים אותם — using הרג, the strong killing verb). Greek: 'with them they do HARM' (ἐν αὐταῖς ἀδικοῦσιν — using ἀδικέω, 'to wrong/harm'). The Hebrew is more severe — these serpent-tails kill, they don't merely injure.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'their power' (כחם — koach, raw might). Greek: 'their authority' (ἐξουσία — delegated authority). Different concept.
Hebrew: 'with these they kill them' (ובאילו הורגים אותם). Greek: 'with them they do harm' (ἐν αὐταῖς ἀδικοῦσιν). Kill vs. harm.
translation_notes: The serpent-tail imagery connects to Genesis 3:15 — the serpent strikes at the heel. Here the serpent-tails attack from behind, an image of treacherous assault consistent with the nachash of Eden.
textual_notes: Numbers 21:6 — 'And YHWH sent fiery serpents (נחשים שרפים) among the people, and they bit the people, and many people of Israel died.' The combination of serpents and death from divine judgment echoes this Revelation passage.

verses.translation: But there were still many{H7227} sons{H1121} of Adam{H120} who were not killed{H4191} by these plagues{H5061}, because they repented of their evil{H7451} deeds{H4639} and did not pray{H6419} to the Satan{H7854}, nor to foreign{H2114} worship{H5656} made of clay{H2789} and stone{H68} or wood{H6086} and silver{H3701} and gold{H2091}, which have no ability to walk{H1980} or speak{H1696} or hear{H8085}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL THEOLOGICAL DIVERGENCE: The Hebrew says survivors were NOT killed BECAUSE (בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁ) they REPENTED (עָשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה). Greek (v20) says the survivors DID NOT repent (οὐ μετενόησαν). These are OPPOSITE theological messages. The Hebrew presents EFFECTIVE judgment — the plagues achieved their purpose of producing repentance, and the repentant were spared. The Greek presents HARDENED HEARTS — the plagues failed to produce repentance. These cannot be translation variants in either direction.

Uses תְּשׁוּבָה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return') — the quintessential Hebrew concept of turning back to God, from the root שׁוּב (shuv, H7725 — 'to return'). This is directional — a physical turning back. Greek μετάνοια ('change of mind') is a cognitive concept. The Hebrew teshuvah carries the full weight of prophetic call-to-return theology (Hos 14:2, Joel 2:12-13, Jer 3:12,14).

Uses הַשָּׂטָן (ha-Satan — 'the Satan/Adversary', H7854) with the definite article — a TITLE meaning 'the Adversary/Accuser' (Job 1:6-12, 2:1-7; Zech 3:1-2; 1 Chr 21:1). Greek has τὰ δαιμόνια ('demons' — plural). The Hebrew mentions the singular Adversary; the Greek mentions plural spirits. These are entirely different theological categories. A back-translator from Greek 'demons' would never write 'the Satan' with the definite article.

Uses עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ('foreign worship', H5656+H2114) — the standard Rabbinic technical term for idol worship (see Mishnah tractate Avodah Zarah). Greek uses τὰ εἴδωλα ('idols'). A back-translator from Greek would use אֱלִילִים (elilim — 'worthless things') or פְּסִילִים (pesilim — 'graven images'), not the Rabbinic legal term.

Uses חֶרֶס (cheres, H2789 — 'clay/earthenware') in the idol materials list. Greek has τὰ χαλκᾶ ('bronze things'). The Hebrew says CLAY; the Greek says BRONZE. A back-translator from Greek would write נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet — 'bronze'), not cheres. The Hebrew lists clay idols — a specifically Mesopotamian type of idol (clay figurines are the most common archaeological finds in Babylon and Assyria).
contradictions: Hebrew: survivors were spared BECAUSE they repented. Greek: survivors did NOT repent. These are directly contradictory theological claims about the efficacy of divine judgment.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'because they repented' (בשביל שעשו תשובה). Greek: 'they did not repent' (οὐ μετενόησαν). Opposite meanings — the most significant textual divergence in this chapter.
Hebrew: 'the Satan' (השטן — singular adversary with article). Greek: 'demons' (δαιμόνια — plural spirits). Singular vs. plural, title vs. class.
Hebrew: 'foreign worship' (עבודה זרה). Greek: 'idols' (εἴδωλα). Different terminology.
Hebrew materials: clay (חרס), stone, wood, silver, gold. Greek: gold, silver, bronze (χαλκᾶ), stone, wood. Different order and clay vs. bronze.
Hebrew disabilities: walk, speak, hear (הלך, דבר, שמע). Greek: see, hear, walk (βλέπειν, ἀκούειν, περιπατεῖν). Hebrew includes 'speak' but not 'see'; Greek includes 'see' but not 'speak.'
translation_notes: 'Because they repented' — the Hebrew בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁ is unambiguous: it means 'because/on account of the fact that.' The survivors lived because of their repentance.
עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (avodah zarah — 'foreign worship/service') is THE standard Rabbinic term for idolatry. It literally means 'strange/alien service' — worship that is foreign to YHWH.
The Hebrew distinguishes two groups: v19 — those spared because they repented; v20 — those who did NOT repent. The Greek lumps all survivors into one category of impenitence.
textual_notes: The idol polemic echoes Psalm 115:4-7: 'They have mouths but do not speak; eyes but do not see; ears but do not hear.' Also Psalm 135:15-17. The Hebrew version lists 'walk, speak, hear' — closer to Daniel 5:23 ('gods of silver and gold, bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know') but with 'speak' substituted for 'see.'

Joel 2:12-14 — 'Return to me with all your heart... rend your hearts and not your garments. Return to YHWH your God, for he is gracious and merciful... Who knows whether he will turn and relent?' The Hebrew Revelation's theology of effective repentance aligns with Joel's call to return.

verses.translation: And those who did not repent of their sorceries{H3785} and their fornications{H2184} or their thefts{H1591}.

one_way_hebrew: The Hebrew distinguishes TWO groups of survivors: v19 — those spared because they repented and abandoned the Satan and idolatry; v20 — those who did NOT repent of sorcery, fornication, and theft. Greek lumps ALL survivors as one group of unrepentant people. The Hebrew presents a more nuanced moral framework that recognizes both repentance and impenitence among the survivors.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'their sorceries and their fornications or their thefts' (3 sins). Greek (v21): 'their murders, their sorceries, their fornication, their thefts' (4 sins — adds φόνων, 'murders'). Hebrew omits 'murders.'
Brackets [  ] in the Hebrew source between 'sorceries' and 'fornications' suggest missing text, possibly corresponding to Greek's additional 'murders.'
translation_notes: כִּשְׁפֵיהֶם (kishfeihem — 'their sorceries', from כשף H3785) — the OT term for witchcraft/sorcery (Ex 22:17, Deut 18:10, 2 Kings 9:22, Mic 5:11, Nah 3:4). Greek φαρμακειῶν ('drug-sorceries') emphasizes the pharmaceutical/potion aspect; the Hebrew kishuf encompasses broader occult practice.
גְּנֵבוֹת (genevot — 'thefts', from גנב H1589/H1591) echoes the Decalogue commandment (Ex 20:15 — לֹא תִּגְנֹב, 'you shall not steal').

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 9 in Hebrew draws massively on Genesis cosmology (tehom/the Deep, used 5 times), the Exodus plague tradition (arbeh/locusts, tannur/furnace), Joel's locust-army imagery (Joel 1:6 verbatim, Joel 2:4 echo), and Torah-specific vocabulary (toqea for shofar-blowing, lehashchit for Flood-destruction, noshech for serpent-biting, rechev for chariotry). The chapter contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers: (1) תהום ('the Deep') for the abyss — the Genesis 1:2 primordial chaos, not ἄβυσσος; (2) 'the great SEA called Euphrates' (ים not נהר) vs. Greek 'the great RIVER'; (3) 'corners of the Temple' vs. 'horns of the golden altar'; (4) 'garments of PITCH' vs. 'breastplates of JACINTH'; (5) 'chariotry' (rechev) vs. 'cavalry armies'; (6) the Hebrew→Greek direction of explanation in v10 ('his name in the Hebrew tongue is Avadon, and in the tongue of Yavan, Apollyon'); (7) the Joel 1:6 verbatim singular שניו ('its teeth') within a plural context; (8) 'tails like a LOCUST' vs. 'tails like SCORPIONS'; (9) כח (koach — raw power) vs. ἐξουσία (exousia — delegated authority). The most critical marker is the theological divergence in v19: the Hebrew says survivors were spared BECAUSE they repented (עשו תשובה), while Greek says they did NOT repent (οὐ μετενόησαν) — directly contradictory claims. Further one-way markers include (10) 'the Satan' (singular with article) vs. 'demons' (plural); (11) עבודה זרה ('foreign worship,' the Rabbinic technical term) vs. 'idols'; and (12) חרס ('clay' — Mesopotamian idol material) vs. χαλκᾶ ('bronze'). The Hebrew text is consistently more concise than the Greek, and several brackets indicate lacunae where the source may be damaged.
